hints: Notice the target reaction forms C2H6 from separate gaseous atoms, so think about which bonds are made and nothing is broken.
Look at the reaction CH4(g) to C(g) + 4H(g) with ΔH = +1648, this tells you the energy to break four C-H bonds, so work out one C-H bond.
Count the bonds made in ethane carefully, one C-C plus six C-H, then combine their bond-making energies with a negative sign.
walkthrough:
**Spot what the target reaction does**

Think simply. We start with 2C(g) + 6H(g) and finish with C2H6(g). No bonds are broken, only new bonds are formed.

$$2\text{C(g)} + 6\text{H(g)} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{(g)}$$

**Find the C-H bond enthalpy**

The table does not give C-H directly, but it gives atomisation of methane. Breaking CH4 into atoms breaks 4 C-H bonds and costs +1648 kJ mol-1.

$$E(\text{C-H}) = \frac{1648}{4} = 412 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**Count bonds in ethane**

Draw or picture CH3-CH3. There is 1 C-C single bond and 6 C-H bonds. From the second table, E(C-C) = 350 kJ mol-1.

$$\text{bonds formed} = 1(\text{C-C}) + 6(\text{C-H})$$

**Apply bonds made means energy released**

Bond formation is exothermic, so ΔH is negative. Add up the energy released.

$$\Delta H = -[E(\text{C-C}) + 6 \times E(\text{C-H})]$$
$$\Delta H = -[350 + 6 \times 412] = -[350 + 2472] = -2822 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

options.A: Correct. One C-C (350) plus six C-H (6 x 412 = 2472) are formed, giving -(350 + 2472) = -2822 kJ mol-1. This is strongly exothermic as expected for forming 7 covalent bonds from atoms.
options.B: Incorrect. This comes from a sign error, doing 6(C-H) minus C-C, i.e. -(2472 - 350) = -2122. Both bonds are formed, so both terms must be added before applying the negative sign.
options.C: Incorrect. This is -(1648 + 350) = -1998. It uses the atomisation energy of only one CH4 (4 C-H bonds) instead of scaling up to the six C-H bonds needed in ethane. Always count bonds in the target molecule.
options.D: Incorrect. This value tries to mix in irrelevant data such as standard enthalpies of formation (-76, -105) or combustion (-890) or H-H (436). Those refer to C(s), H2(g) and O2(g), not to the gaseous atoms C(g) and H(g) in this question, so they cannot be used directly here.
